title: The thousand names held back
hookLine: Hayagriva leaves out Lalita's thousand names until Agastya asks
carry: a guru guards the practice; devotion opens the door
tomorrow: a city of walls, and red powder at the edge. why start there?

cards: The sage Agastya sits at the feet of his teacher, Hayagriva, Vishnu with the head of a horse.
Day after day Hayagriva tells him about the Goddess Lalita: how she rose from the gods' sacred fire, the battles she won, the city built for her. Then the teaching ends, and Agastya is troubled.
Something is missing: her thousand names. Why leave them out? In the frame of the Lalita Sahasranama, Hayagriva answers: these names are kept close, given only to those who come with devotion.
And because you've asked with devotion, I'll give them to you now. So who gets to walk all the way in? People who love this yantra answer two ways.

teach.b: First, where they're walking to. At the very center of the Sri Yantra sits a dot, the bindu, a drop or a point. One of Lalita's thousand names calls her the one seated in the bindu.
The gates, lotuses and woven triangles are rooms of a house; the bindu is where she's at home. Now the two voices.
First: in Hinduism the deepest practices pass from guru to student, teacher to disciple, in an unbroken line.
In Sri Vidya lineages, the full worship of the yantra and its mantra are received through initiation, called diksha.
The best case: the road passes through every layer in order, and someone who has walked it can walk you through. Even Hayagriva didn't hand out the names to just anyone.
Second: those same thousand names, once held back, are now chanted in homes and temples everywhere, often by people with no initiation at all.
The best case: Agastya was given the names because he asked with devotion, and a mother's house isn't locked to children who ask. Notice what each protects. The first guards the depth.
Both rest on one moment: a teacher who guards, and a student who asks with love.

how: In Sri Vidya lineages the full worship of the Sri Yantra and its mantra are given by a teacher through initiation (diksha); in other homes, people keep a yantra and offer flowers or kumkum while reciting the Lalita Sahasranama.

Sri Vidya lineages give it through diksha; in many homes, her names are chanted freely.

games.q: a friend's family wants to keep a Sri Yantra at home, but a teacher they know says the full worship needs initiation. which reply gives both sides their best case?
o: the teacher guards the depth; the open home guards the welcome. Agastya's story holds both.
the teacher is just gatekeeping; the gates face every way, so ignore him.
home devotion doesn't count; without initiation the yantra is only decoration.
games.why: Hayagriva guarded the names and gave them to a student who asked with devotion. one voice protects the depth, the other the welcome; both love the same point.

practice: Make a small dot on a piece of paper, or pick one point in front of you. Before you begin, bow your head for a moment to someone who taught you something that mattered; many Hindus begin their practice by honoring their guru.
Then let your gaze rest on the point, and let everything around it go soft. Each time the eyes wander, come back to the one point.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Yantra's center: the bindu, a point with no size, where the Goddess is said to sit and where every line ends.

orig.note: Sanskrit bindu, a drop or point: the yantra's center, the Goddess's seat.
